title: Pagan animal customs
def: The Quran condemns pagan Arab customs of dedicating certain animals to their gods (5:103).
what: “God has not made any baḥīra, sāʾiba, waṣīla or ḥām; but those who disbelieve invent a lie against God” (5:103). They were camels set free or exempted from use as offerings to idols. The Quran counts this among the false rules made by the Meccans in their religion (6:138–139).

title: Parables
def: The Quran teaches through similes, including that of a gnat (2:26), a grain that multiplies (2:261) and a spider’s house (29:41).
what: “God is not ashamed to strike a parable of a gnat or something above it” (2:26). “The likeness of those who spend their wealth in God’s way is like a grain that grows seven ears, in each ear a hundred grains” (2:261). “The likeness of those who take protectors besides God is that of the spider, which builds a house; the frailest of houses is the spider’s house” (29:41). A good word is “like a good tree, its root firm and its branches in the sky” (14:24).

title: Paradise
def: The garden of the righteous, described in the Quran with gardens, rivers, companions and, above all, God’s good pleasure.
what: “Gardens of Eden beneath which rivers flow” (9:72), where the people of Paradise are “adorned with bracelets of gold and pearls, and their clothing is silk” (35:33). They drink from cups “mixed with ginger” (76:17) and from vessels of silver and crystal (76:15–16). They will have “no idle talk”, but “peace” (56:25–26). “Their greeting is peace” (10:10). The greatest of the rewards is God’s good pleasure (9:72).
misread: That Islam’s Paradise is only sensual.
sources: The Prophet said that God has prepared for His righteous servants “what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has imagined” (Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim). Scholars read the images of food and drink as made known to us in terms we understand. On whether the garden of Adam was this Paradise, Muslim scholars differ: most say it was, and some, among them Abu Hanifa’s followers and the Mu’tazilites, say it was a garden on earth.

title: People of the Heights
def: Those on the elevations (al-aʿrāf) between Paradise and Hell on the Day of Judgement (7:46–49).
what: “Between them is a veil, and on the heights are men who know each by his mark” (7:46). They greet the people of Paradise, and speak to the people of Hell. Commentators differ on who they are: some say those whose good and bad deeds are balanced, others the righteous or prophets. The chapter that mentions them, al-A’raf, is the seventh.

title: Pre-Islamic Arab deities
def: The idols the Meccans worshipped: al-Lat, al-Uzza and Manat, and Wadd, Suwa, Yaghuth, Yauq and Nasr, named in the Quran.
what: The Quran asks: “Have you considered al-Lat and al-Uzza, and Manat, the third, the other?” (53:19–20). Noah’s people are said to have worshipped Wadd, Suwa, Yaghuth, Yauq and Nasr (71:23). Hubal was the chief idol in the Kaaba. The Quran says that these “are but names which you and your fathers have named; God has sent down no authority for them” (53:23).
misread: That the Prophet once recited verses allowing prayer to these goddesses (the “Satanic verses”).
sources: The story of the “high-flying cranes” (gharānīq) is told in the biography of Ibn Sa’d and in al-Tabari, with chains that are broken. Hadith scholars such as Ibn Hajar and al-Albani judged them unsound, and Qadi Iyad and others refuted the story. The verse sometimes cited for it (22:52) is explained by most commentators as saying that Satan throws doubts and obstacles in the way of a prophet’s mission, and that God removes them; it does not say that he adds words to revelation. The Quran says of the Prophet that “he does not speak from desire” (53:3).
aliases: Gods Of Pre-Islamic Arabs By Name

title: Prisoners of war
def: The Quran’s rule for prisoners taken in battle: release them with grace or for ransom (47:4).
what: “When you meet those who disbelieve, strike their necks until you have subdued them, then bind the captives firmly, and afterwards either release them as a favour or for ransom, until the war lays down its burdens” (47:4). After Badr, the question of the prisoners was disputed: Abu Bakr advised ransom and Umar execution, and 8:67 says a prophet should not take captives until he has fully established himself in the land (Sahih Muslim). The prisoners were afterwards ransomed.
sources: The Prophet is reported to have told the Companions to treat the prisoners well, and the Companions gave them the better of their own food (Ibn Hisham). Classical jurists listed further options, including enslavement and, in some schools, execution, drawing on later practice. Many contemporary scholars hold that the Quran’s own two options bind.
